Evan Murray Portland LD 10
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and members of the Judiciary committee,
I am writing to ask you to oppose LD 10: An Act to Add Political Affiliation as a Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act.
I am generally in favor of protecting people from discrimination, but this is written too broadly; rather than combat a genuine problem, it will open the door to claims of discrimination. From what I've seen, supporters of this bill believe it is necessary to protect conservative people from discrimination based on their political beliefs; I suspect they have not thought about other groups who could claim equal protection under it.
The Ku Klux Klan is a political organization, after all. Almost anything can be deemed a political affiliation, because politics touches every area of our lives.
As written, this bill would allow anyone with a grievance to claim political discrimination, clogging our courts and increasing rather than decreasing political divisions among members of the public. I believe it would create far more problems than it would solve.
Thank you.

Testimony of Senator James D. Libby

"An Act to Add Political Affiliation as a Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act."
Public Hearing, Tuesday, February 5, 2025
State House Building, 438
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and esteemed members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary,
My name is Jim Libby, and I am a State Senator representing Senate District # 22, comprised of the towns of
Naples, Sebago, Baldwin, and Standish in Cumberland County; Hiram and Porter in Oxford County; and, Limington, Limerick, Cornish, Parsonsfield, Newfield, Acton, and Shapleigh, in the County of York.
It is my honor to bring to your attention the contents of LD 10 "An Act to Add Political Affiliation as a
Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act."
As you know, a protected class is a group of people intended by a legislature to benefit from the protection of a
statute. Thanks to federal civil rights law, discrimination is prohibited on the basis of race, sex, religion, national origin, and so forth.
States have gone further in the development of protections in labor function. According to Nolo.com,
"discrimination based on politics happens when an employer makes job decisions because of an employee's
political beliefs, party affiliation, or civic activities. An employer that, for example, refuses to hire applicants
who vote [Democrat or] Republican, fires anyone who supports [or opposes] gun control, or demotes someone who runs for the local school board is engaged in political discrimination."
Did you know that over 60 million people already enjoy this right that I bring for your consideration today?
States like California and New York have added political affiliation to their protected class groups.
Where are we in Maine on this issue? Keep in mind that when companies in Maine train employees on
discrimination, political activity is included in the training, but the training ends up making excuses for the
states who have not adopted political discrimination into their statutes. That is too bad for Maine.
I first became aware of this issue as a result of completing a human resources training video at my employer.
In that video, the benefits are presented as important. The training video is widely used in Maine already. The
video is from Vector LMS Higher Education Edition, and it is called "Preventing Harassment and

Discrimination: Non-Supervisors Clery Act and Title IX."
The fact is that adding this protection is 100% non-partisan. People on both sides of the aisle in other states welcome this protection. These citizens do not need to fear being fired for participating in their community and
taking a position, left, right, or center.
An exception is created for a situation in which a job description specifies that part of a job includes partisan
activity. That is perfectly fine. The idea is along the same lines as a job description that requires the ability to lift a certain amount of weight.
I believe that this protection will be added to Maine civil rights law someday soon, because it removes a layer of heightened tensions among Maine citizens. If not you, if not today, then someday soon. Society has
changed. We need to protect workers from these kinds of actions - firings that bend and break civility, even
morality. I am talking about your constituents back home who today fear that speaking up on issues outside of
the workplace will cost them their jobs.
Please give this bill your strongest consideration. It is an issue that will come back again and again, until we
fully embrace it.
Thank you for your consideration of this legislation.

Re: An Act to Add Political Affiliation as a Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act - LD 10
Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary:

The Maine Human Rights Commission ("Commission") is Maine's quasi-independent, nonpartisan State agency charged with enforcing our state anti-discrimination law, the Maine Human Rights Act, 5 M.R.S. �� 4551, et seq. ("MHRA"). The Commission is statutorily charged with the duties of: investigating, conciliating, and at times litigating protected-class discrimination cases under the MHRA; promulgating rules and regulations to effectuate the Act; and making recommendations for further legislation or executive action concerning infringements on human rights in
Maine. 5 M.R.S. � 4566(7), (11). With those duties in mind, the Commission is pleased to provide this testimony neither for nor against LD 1663.
The MHRA addresses adverse treatment against individuals based primarily upon their innate characteristics
(things one does not choose about oneself). "Political affiliation" might be an outlier within the MHRA's current framework. The proposed subsection 8-I definition of who would be a member of the protected class is exceedingly broad; "political affiliation" would "mean belonging to or endorsing a party or a particular political philosophy, creed or
ideal." Adopting this definition would provide MHRA protected-class status to anyone who endorsed any political idea.
Given what would be LD 10's wide scope of coverage, the Commission anticipates that it would receive significant numbers of complaints related to political affiliation; the Commission's fiscal note reflects this foreseeable impact on
the agency's operations.
Thank you for this opportunity to provide testimony about LD 10. The Commission would be pleased to discuss these issues with you at your convenience, including at the work session on this matter.

Sincerely,

River Knight Biddeford ME LD 10
LD 10 (2025) -- An Act to Add Political Affiliation as a Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act
Senator Libby and the judiciary. My name is River Knight. I go to the alternative pathways center in Biddeford ME As a student, I strongly support an Act to Add Political Affiliation as a Protected Class to the Maine Human Rights Act. Students are encouraged to engage in civic life, learn about government, and form our own political beliefs. However, many young people fear that expressing those beliefs could negatively affect future employment, housing, or educational opportunities. That fear discourages participation and weakens our democracy. Political affiliation is a deeply personal aspect of identity, especially for students who are still learning how to engage thoughtfully and responsibly in public discourse. No one should face discrimination for their political views simply for participating in the democratic process. By adding political affiliation as a protected class, Maine sends a clear message that respectful disagreement is not a reason for exclusion or punishment. This law would help ensure that students can learn, grow, and participate in civic life without fear of discrimination. I urge you to support this legislation and protect the rights of current and future generations of Mainers. Sincerley, River Knight
